prompt: A postoperative patient on room air has pH 7.28, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, and HCO3- 26 mEq/L after a large opioid dose. How should the therapist interpret this gas?

options.text: Acute respiratory acidosis without renal compensation
Chronic respiratory acidosis with full renal compensation
Metabolic acidosis with partial respiratory compensation
Combined respiratory and metabolic acidosis

explanation: pH below 7.35 with PaCO2 above 45 points to respiratory acidosis. In acute retention HCO3- rises only about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg of PaCO2, so 26 is the expected acute value: no meaningful compensation yet, which fits opioid hypoventilation.

distractorExplanations.b: Chronic retention raises HCO3- about 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg (to roughly 31) and brings pH close to 7.35.
distractorExplanations.c: Metabolic acidosis needs a low HCO3-; here HCO3- is normal and PaCO2 is high, the opposite of respiratory compensation.
distractorExplanations.d: A combined acidosis would show a high PaCO2 and a low HCO3-; 26 mEq/L is inside the normal range.

prompt: A patient with long-standing COPD, at baseline, has pH 7.36, PaCO2 62 mm Hg, HCO3- 34 mEq/L, and PaO2 58 mm Hg on 1 L/min. Which interpretation fits?

options.text: Acute-on-chronic ventilatory failure that needs intubation now
Compensated respiratory acidosis from chronic CO2 retention
Partly compensated metabolic alkalosis
Mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis

explanation: PaCO2 is high and pH sits on the acid side of 7.40, so the primary process is respiratory acidosis; the kidneys have retained enough HCO3- to bring pH back into range. This is the expected baseline of a chronic CO2 retainer and is not by itself a reason to intubate.

distractorExplanations.a: Acute failure would show a pH well below 7.35; a near-normal pH means the hypercapnia is chronic and compensated.
distractorExplanations.c: If metabolic alkalosis were primary the pH would be above 7.40; here pH 7.36 follows the high PaCO2.
distractorExplanations.d: A mixed acidosis would have a low HCO3-; 34 mEq/L is raised, which is compensation, not a second acidosis.

prompt: An anxious patient in the emergency department has pH 7.51, PaCO2 29 mm Hg, HCO3- 23 mEq/L, and tingling fingers. What is the interpretation?

options.text: Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
Compensated respiratory alkalosis
Acute respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation

explanation: An alkalemic pH with a low PaCO2 identifies respiratory alkalosis. HCO3- 23 is essentially normal, so the kidneys have not compensated yet and the process is acute. Rule out hypoxemia or pulmonary embolism before attributing it to anxiety.

distractorExplanations.a: Metabolic alkalosis needs a raised HCO3- and is compensated by a rising, not falling, PaCO2.
distractorExplanations.b: Renal compensation would lower HCO3- to roughly 18-20 and pull pH toward 7.45; neither has happened.
distractorExplanations.d: Primary metabolic acidosis gives an acidemic pH and a low HCO3-; this pH is alkalemic.

prompt: At sea level (PB 760 mm Hg) a patient breathing room air has PaO2 60 mm Hg and PaCO2 40 mm Hg. What is the approximate alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient?

options.text: About 40 mm Hg
About 50 mm Hg
About 90 mm Hg
About 100 mm Hg

explanation: PAO2 = 0.21 x (760 - 47) - 40/0.8, about 150 - 50 = 100 mm Hg. Subtracting the PaO2 of 60 gives about 40 mm Hg, well above the normal 5-15 mm Hg on room air, so the hypoxemia is not from hypoventilation alone.

distractorExplanations.b: 50 mm Hg subtracts PaCO2 without dividing it by the 0.8 respiratory quotient.
distractorExplanations.c: 90 mm Hg leaves out the PaCO2 term entirely (150 - 60) and overstates the gradient.
distractorExplanations.d: 100 mm Hg is the alveolar PO2 itself; the gradient subtracts the arterial PaO2 of 60.

prompt: A ventilated patient with bilateral infiltrates not explained by heart failure has PaO2 75 mm Hg on FiO2 0.50 with PEEP 10 cm H2O. How is ARDS severity graded under the Berlin definition?

options.text: No ARDS, because PaO2 is above 60 mm Hg
Mild ARDS (P/F ratio 201-300)
Moderate ARDS (P/F ratio 101-200)
Severe ARDS (P/F ratio 100 or less)

explanation: P/F = 75 / 0.50 = 150, inside the 101-200 band for moderate ARDS with PEEP of at least 5 cm H2O. Severity is graded by the PaO2/FiO2 ratio, not raw PaO2, so a PaO2 that looks acceptable can still hide a large shunt on high FiO2.

distractorExplanations.a: Raw PaO2 does not define ARDS; the ratio to FiO2 does, and 150 meets the criteria.
distractorExplanations.b: Mild ARDS needs a P/F above 200; 75 divided by 0.50 is 150.
distractorExplanations.d: Severe ARDS is a P/F of 100 or less; 150 is better than that cutoff.

prompt: A volume-controlled patient has VT 500 mL, PIP 45 cm H2O, plateau pressure 30 cm H2O, and PEEP 10 cm H2O. What is the static compliance?

options.text: About 14 mL/cm H2O
About 17 mL/cm H2O
About 25 mL/cm H2O
About 50 mL/cm H2O

explanation: Static compliance = VT / (Pplat - PEEP) = 500 / (30 - 10) = 25 mL/cm H2O. Plateau pressure is measured with no flow, so it reflects lung and chest-wall stiffness rather than airway resistance. Ventilated adults normally run about 40-100.

distractorExplanations.a: 14 uses PIP (500 / 35); that is dynamic compliance, which includes airway resistance.
distractorExplanations.b: 17 divides by plateau pressure without subtracting PEEP (500 / 30).
distractorExplanations.d: 50 divides by PEEP alone (500 / 10) and ignores the plateau pressure.

prompt: Over one hour a volume-controlled patient's PIP rises from 30 to 42 cm H2O while plateau pressure stays at 25 cm H2O. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: A pneumothorax reducing lung compliance
A leak in the expiratory limb of the circuit
Worsening pulmonary edema that is stiffening the lung tissue
Higher airway resistance from secretions or bronchospasm

explanation: PIP minus plateau is the pressure spent overcoming airway resistance. A gap widening from 5 to 17 cm H2O with a stable plateau points to the airways: secretions, bronchospasm, or a kinked or bitten tube. Suction, check the tube, and listen for wheeze.

distractorExplanations.a: A pneumothorax lowers compliance, so plateau pressure would rise along with PIP.
distractorExplanations.b: A circuit leak lowers pressures and sets off low-pressure or low-volume alarms.
distractorExplanations.c: Edema stiffens the lung and raises plateau pressure; here plateau is unchanged.

Bronchospasm in a patient with a history of asthma
A mucus plug partly blocking the tube
The patient biting down on the tube

distractorExplanations.c: A plug in the tube is a resistance problem; plateau would stay near 24.
distractorExplanations.d: Biting the tube raises PIP through resistance; plateau would not climb with it.

Left lower-lobe atelectasis with volume loss
Left tension pneumothorax
Left lower-lobe pneumonia without any lobar collapse

prompt: Spirometry shows FEV1/FVC 0.58 and FEV1 55% of predicted. After albuterol, FEV1 rises by 6% and 90 mL. How should the result be reported?

Restriction confirmed by spirometry alone
Obstruction with a significant bronchodilator response
A normal study that was limited by suboptimal patient effort

explanation: A reduced FEV1/FVC (below 0.70 or the lower limit of normal) defines obstruction. A significant response has traditionally needed at least 12% and 200 mL of improvement; 6% and 90 mL falls short. The pattern fits COPD better than asthma.

distractorExplanations.b: Restriction needs a low TLC on lung volumes; a low FEV1/FVC points to obstruction.
distractorExplanations.c: 6% and 90 mL is below the 12% and 200 mL threshold for a significant response.
distractorExplanations.d: A ratio of 0.58 from an acceptable test is a real obstructive finding, not an effort artifact.

prompt: A dyspneic patient has normal spirometry and lung volumes, but DLCO is 48% of predicted with a normal hemoglobin. Which condition best fits?

Chronic bronchitis
Pulmonary hypertension or other vascular disease
Neuromuscular weakness from generalized myasthenia gravis

explanation: An isolated low DLCO with normal mechanics and hemoglobin points to loss of pulmonary capillary bed: pulmonary hypertension, chronic thromboembolic disease, or early interstitial disease. Echocardiography or a V/Q scan is a sensible next recommendation.

Start hourly incentive spirometry

Elective intubation and mechanical ventilation

prompt: A patient rescued from a house fire has an SpO2 of 98% by pulse oximetry, a headache, and soot in the nares. What should the therapist recommend first?

Measure COHb by CO-oximetry and give 100% oxygen
Order a chest radiograph before giving oxygen
Apply 2 L/min nasal cannula and recheck SpO2 in 15 minutes

explanation: Standard two-wavelength oximeters read carboxyhemoglobin as oxyhemoglobin, so SpO2 overstates true saturation after smoke inhalation. Start 100% oxygen by non-rebreather (intubate if the airway is threatened) and confirm the COHb level by CO-oximetry.

Metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap
Acute respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis

52 mEq/L

prompt: Raising FiO2 from 0.40 to 1.0 increases a patient's PaO2 only from 52 to 58 mm Hg. Which mechanism best explains this?

options.text: Ventilation-perfusion mismatch
Alveolar hypoventilation
Intrapulmonary shunt
Diffusion impairment

explanation: Blood that passes unventilated alveoli never meets the added oxygen, so shunt hypoxemia barely responds to FiO2. Refractory hypoxemia like this calls for alveolar recruitment with PEEP or CPAP rather than more oxygen.

distractorExplanations.a: V/Q mismatch responds well to a higher FiO2; PaO2 would climb much further.
distractorExplanations.b: Hypoventilation hypoxemia corrects easily with modest supplemental oxygen.
distractorExplanations.d: Diffusion defects respond to oxygen because the driving pressure across the membrane rises.

prompt: On a ventilated COPD patient's flow-time graphic, expiratory flow does not return to zero before the next breath begins. What does this indicate?

options.text: Air trapping with intrinsic PEEP (auto-PEEP)
A large leak around the endotracheal tube cuff
Patient effort triggering extra breaths
Normal expiration in volume control

explanation: Flow still moving when the next breath starts means the lung has not emptied to its relaxed volume. Measure auto-PEEP with an expiratory hold, then lengthen expiratory time: lower the rate or VT, raise inspiratory flow, and treat bronchospasm.

distractorExplanations.b: A cuff leak shows returned volume below delivered volume, not truncated expiratory flow.
distractorExplanations.c: Patient triggering shows a negative deflection before the breath, not unfinished exhalation.
distractorExplanations.d: Expiratory flow should reach zero before the next breath; this is not normal.

prompt: A patient has Hb 15 g/dL, SaO2 98%, and PaO2 100 mm Hg. What is the arterial oxygen content (CaO2)?

options.text: About 0.3 mL O2/dL
About 14.7 mL O2/dL
About 20.0 mL O2/dL
About 49.7 mL O2/dL

explanation: CaO2 = (1.34 x Hb x SaO2) + (0.003 x PaO2) = (1.34 x 15 x 0.98) + 0.3, about 19.7 + 0.3 = 20.0 mL O2/dL. Nearly all oxygen rides on hemoglobin; the dissolved share is tiny at a normal PaO2.

distractorExplanations.a: 0.3 is only the dissolved oxygen (0.003 x 100) and ignores hemoglobin-bound oxygen.
distractorExplanations.b: 14.7 multiplies Hb by SaO2 but leaves out the 1.34 mL O2 carried per gram of hemoglobin.
distractorExplanations.d: 49.7 uses 0.3 instead of 0.003 for dissolved oxygen, overstating it a hundredfold.

prompt: A term newborn on 100% oxygen has a preductal SpO2 of 95% and a postductal SpO2 of 82%. Which condition does this difference suggest?

options.text: Respiratory distress syndrome from surfactant deficiency
Transient tachypnea of the newborn
A pulse oximeter probe malfunction
Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn

explanation: A preductal-postductal difference of more than about 10% shows right-to-left shunting across the ductus arteriosus, typical of PPHN. Recommend echocardiography; management includes optimal oxygenation and ventilation and inhaled nitric oxide.

distractorExplanations.a: RDS lowers oxygenation at both sites; it does not by itself create a pre/postductal gap.
distractorExplanations.b: TTN is mild, settles in 1-2 days, and does not cause ductal shunting.
distractorExplanations.c: A 13-point gap between two good-signal sites is physiology; rechecking is fine, but the pattern is classic PPHN.

Nocturnal oxygen only
Oxygen titrated for ambulation
Stopping all exercise until SpO2 improves

prompt: An E cylinder (factor 0.28 L/psi) reads 2,000 psi. How long will it last at 2 L/min if the whole contents are used?

About 140 minutes
About 210 minutes
About 280 minutes

explanation: Duration = (gauge pressure x cylinder factor) / flow = (2,000 x 0.28) / 2 = 280 minutes. In practice a reserve (often 200-500 psi) is kept, so plan a transport for less time than the full figure.

About 48 L/min
About 88 L/min

prompt: A ventilated patient's heated humidifier circuit shows heavy condensation pooling in the inspiratory limb. What should the therapist do?

options.text: Drain the condensate back into the heated humidifier chamber
Switch to an HME even though secretions are thick
Drain it away from the patient; adjust heated-wire settings
Turn the humidifier off until the circuit dries out

explanation: Rainout forms when gas cools along the circuit. Drain it into a trap away from the patient, never back into the reservoir, and adjust the chamber and heated-wire temperatures so the gas does not cool on its way to the Y-piece.

distractorExplanations.b: Thick secretions are a contraindication to an HME, which adds less humidity than active heating.

prompt: Which ventilated patient is the poorest candidate for a heat-and-moisture exchanger (HME) instead of a heated humidifier?

options.text: A post-op patient expected to extubate within 12 hours
A patient with thick, bloody secretions and a large cuff leak
A patient being transported briefly from the ICU to CT
A ventilated adult with thin, scant secretions and no cuff leak

explanation: An HME returns only part of the exhaled heat and moisture. It is contraindicated with thick or bloody secretions (they can occlude it), large leaks (exhaled moisture never reaches it), hypothermia, and very high minute ventilation; use active humidification instead.

distractorExplanations.a: Short-term ventilation after surgery is a classic HME use.
distractorExplanations.c: Brief transport is a common and appropriate HME setting.
distractorExplanations.d: Thin, scant secretions without a leak make an HME suitable.

Add 3 mL more saline to the cup
Replace the nebulizer because it is a faulty unit
Tap the cup once, then end the treatment

prompt: A galvanic fuel-cell oxygen analyzer reads 18% when exposed to room air. What should the therapist do?

options.text: Recalibrate at 21% and 100%; replace the cell if it drifts
Accept it, because fuel-cell analyzers read 3% low at sea level
Add 3% to every reading taken with that analyzer
Switch the analyzer into its polarographic sensing mode

explanation: Room air should read 21%. A two-point calibration (21% and 100%) corrects drift; a fuel cell that will not hold calibration is depleted. Also check for moisture on the sensor, which lowers readings.

distractorExplanations.b: Analyzers have no built-in 3% offset; 18% means drift or a failing cell.
distractorExplanations.c: Manually correcting readings is not quality control, and the error may not be linear.
distractorExplanations.d: Galvanic and polarographic are different sensor types, not a selectable mode.

prompt: A ventilator's low-pressure and low exhaled-volume alarms sound together, and the patient is in distress. What should the therapist do first?

Silence the alarm and recheck in 5 minutes
Bag manually with 100% O2 and look for the leak
Lower the low-pressure alarm threshold so it stops sounding

prompt: A ventilated patient's cuff pressure measures 44 cm H2O by manometer. What is the main concern and the correct action?

options.text: Aspiration risk; add more air to the cuff
Tracheal ischemia; reduce to 20-30 cm H2O
A cuff leak; replace the endotracheal tube
A normal reading that needs no further action

explanation: Cuff pressure above about 30 cm H2O can exceed tracheal capillary perfusion pressure and cause ischemia, stenosis, or tracheomalacia. Keep it at 20-30 cm H2O, enough to limit micro-aspiration without injuring the mucosa.

distractorExplanations.a: 44 cm H2O is already too high; more air worsens mucosal injury.
distractorExplanations.c: A high pressure points to over-inflation, not a leak.
distractorExplanations.d: The recommended range is 20-30 cm H2O; 44 is excessive.

Increase the dose to four puffs at once
Remove the valved holding chamber
Give one puff at a time, then breathe

Increase IPAP to widen the pressure support
Increase FiO2 to 0.60
Change to CPAP at 5 cm H2O

explanation: Ventilation on bilevel depends on the IPAP-EPAP difference (pressure support). Raising IPAP increases tidal volume and CO2 clearance. EPAP mainly helps oxygenation, upper-airway patency, and offsetting auto-PEEP.

distractorExplanations.a: Raising EPAP alone narrows the IPAP-EPAP gap and can reduce ventilation.
distractorExplanations.c: Oxygenation is already on target; more FiO2 does not lower PaCO2.
distractorExplanations.d: CPAP gives no inspiratory support to clear CO2.

prompt: An albuterol MDI is ordered for a ventilated patient. Which technique gives the best delivery?

options.text: Actuate it into the expiratory limb of the ventilator circuit
Fire several puffs rapidly at the Y-piece
Remove the HME and actuate with no spacer
Use an inline spacer; actuate as inspiration starts

explanation: An inline spacer in the inspiratory limb near the Y-piece, actuated at the start of inspiration, gets the most drug to the lungs. Remove or bypass the HME, which traps aerosol, and wait between puffs.

distractorExplanations.a: Drug released in the expiratory limb leaves the circuit without reaching the patient.
distractorExplanations.b: Rapid actuations reduce delivery; puffs should be spaced at least 15 seconds apart.
distractorExplanations.c: Removing the HME is correct, but delivery without a spacer is far lower.

prompt: A patient using an inhaled corticosteroid complains of hoarseness and white patches in the mouth. What should the therapist recommend?

options.text: A spacer, and rinse and spit after each dose
Stopping the inhaled steroid permanently
Switching to a long-acting beta agonist alone
Doubling the steroid dose to control symptoms

explanation: Oral candidiasis and dysphonia come from steroid deposited in the oropharynx. A spacer or valved holding chamber and rinsing after each dose reduce local effects; thrush is treated as prescribed.

distractorExplanations.b: Stopping controller therapy risks asthma control when the side effect is preventable.
distractorExplanations.c: LABA monotherapy in asthma raises the risk of severe events.
distractorExplanations.d: A higher dose increases local side effects.

prompt: A ventilated patient has complete left-lung collapse from a suspected mucus plug that persists despite suctioning and chest physiotherapy. What should the therapist recommend?

Increase FiO2 to 1.0 and observe
Therapeutic fiberoptic bronchoscopy
Start an oral mucolytic three times daily

prompt: A 27-week preterm infant on CPAP 6 cm H2O needs FiO2 0.45, with grunting and retractions, and the radiograph shows ground-glass lungs. What should the therapist recommend?

Surfactant administration
Begin inhaled nitric oxide at 20 ppm
Start nebulized albuterol every 4 hours

explanation: This is RDS from surfactant deficiency. Preterm infants on CPAP who need a rising FiO2 (commonly above 0.30-0.40) should receive surfactant, by intubation or a less-invasive technique, and then continue CPAP.

prompt: During adult CPR with an endotracheal tube in place, how should ventilations be delivered?

options.text: 1 breath every 3 seconds during compressions
1 breath every 6 seconds; compressions continue
1 breath every 10 seconds with a pause for each breath
2 breaths after every 30 compressions, pausing each time

explanation: With an advanced airway, compressions continue without pauses at 100-120/min and the rescuer gives 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min). Excess ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return.

distractorExplanations.a: Every 3 seconds (20/min) overventilates an adult in cardiac arrest.
distractorExplanations.c: Compressions should not pause for breaths once an advanced airway is in place.
distractorExplanations.d: 30:2 with pauses applies before an advanced airway is placed.

prompt: During adult CPR, waveform capnography shows an ETCO2 of 8 mm Hg. What does this suggest?

options.text: Poor compressions; improve depth and rate or swap rescuers
Return of spontaneous circulation
Good-quality compressions that should simply continue unchanged
An endotracheal tube that has slipped into the right mainstem

explanation: ETCO2 during CPR reflects pulmonary blood flow. Values below 10 mm Hg suggest poor compressions; improve depth (5-6 cm), rate (100-120/min), and recoil, and change compressors. An abrupt rise to 35-40 mm Hg or more suggests ROSC.

distractorExplanations.b: ROSC causes an abrupt rise in ETCO2, typically to 35-40 mm Hg or more.
distractorExplanations.c: Effective CPR usually produces an ETCO2 above 10-20 mm Hg.
distractorExplanations.d: Mainstem intubation still returns a CO2 waveform and does not explain such a low value.

prompt: Immediately after an emergency intubation, which method most reliably confirms tracheal placement?

options.text: Fogging seen inside the tube
Sustained waveform capnography
A chest radiograph read by the team
Equal chest rise with each bag breath

explanation: Continuous waveform capnography showing CO2 over several breaths is the most reliable bedside confirmation. A chest radiograph checks depth but cannot reliably tell tracheal from esophageal placement.

distractorExplanations.a: Fogging can also occur with esophageal intubation.
distractorExplanations.c: A radiograph checks tube depth and may miss esophageal placement.
distractorExplanations.d: Chest rise can mislead, especially in obese patients.

prompt: A term newborn is still apneic after drying and stimulation, with a heart rate of 80/min. According to NRP, what should be done next?

options.text: Start chest compressions at a 3:1 ratio
Give blow-by oxygen and reassess in a minute
Give epinephrine through an umbilical venous line
Start positive-pressure ventilation

explanation: Apnea, gasping, or a heart rate under 100 after the initial steps calls for positive-pressure ventilation within the first minute of life. Effective ventilation is the single most important step in newborn resuscitation.

distractorExplanations.a: Compressions start only if HR stays below 60 after 30 seconds of effective PPV.
distractorExplanations.b: Blow-by oxygen does not ventilate an apneic infant.
distractorExplanations.c: Epinephrine is for HR below 60 despite effective PPV and compressions.

prompt: After 30 seconds of effective PPV with good chest rise, a newborn's heart rate is 50/min. What is the next step?

options.text: Secure an airway, compress 3:1, and raise FiO2 to 1.0
Continue PPV alone and recheck HR in 2 minutes
Give naloxone through the umbilical venous line
Start chest compressions at a 15:2 ratio with PPV breaths

explanation: HR below 60 after 30 seconds of effective ventilation calls for chest compressions coordinated 3:1 with ventilation (90 compressions and 30 breaths a minute), an advanced airway, and FiO2 raised to 1.0.

distractorExplanations.b: Waiting 2 minutes with HR below 60 delays required compressions.
distractorExplanations.c: Naloxone is not part of routine newborn resuscitation.
distractorExplanations.d: 15:2 is the two-rescuer pediatric ratio, not the newborn ratio.

prompt: At 3 minutes of life, a term infant receiving PPV in room air has a preductal SpO2 of 72%. What should the therapist do with the oxygen?

options.text: Increase FiO2 to 1.0 immediately
Decrease FiO2 to below 0.21
Keep the FiO2; 70-75% is the 3-minute target
Remove the oximeter, as readings are unreliable this early

explanation: NRP preductal targets rise gradually: 60-65% at 1 minute, 70-75% at 3 minutes, 80-85% at 5 minutes, and 85-95% at 10 minutes. A reading of 72% at 3 minutes is on target, so room air continues.

distractorExplanations.a: Jumping to 100% oxygen risks hyperoxia in an infant who is on target.
distractorExplanations.b: FiO2 cannot go below 0.21, and this infant is not hyperoxic.
distractorExplanations.d: Preductal oximetry on the right hand is the recommended guide.

prompt: A newborn delivered through meconium-stained fluid is not vigorous (poor tone, apneic). What does current NRP guidance recommend?

options.text: Intubate and suction the trachea before any breaths
Initial steps, then PPV if apneic or HR under 100
Suction the stomach first to remove swallowed meconium
Wait 1 minute for spontaneous breathing to start

explanation: Since 2015, NRP has not recommended routine intubation for tracheal suction in non-vigorous infants with meconium. Complete the initial steps and start PPV promptly; intubate and suction only if the airway is obstructed.

distractorExplanations.a: Routine tracheal suction delays ventilation and is no longer recommended.
distractorExplanations.c: Gastric suction does nothing for ventilation.
distractorExplanations.d: Waiting delays essential PPV in an apneic infant.

prompt: A ventilated trauma patient suddenly develops high peak pressures, absent left breath sounds, a trachea shifted to the right, and BP 70/40. What is the immediate treatment?

Higher PEEP to support the blood pressure
A larger tidal volume to re-expand the lung
Needle decompression of the left chest

explanation: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. With hemodynamic collapse, needle decompression followed by a chest tube must happen at once; waiting for imaging can be fatal.

distractorExplanations.b: More PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure and worsens hypotension.

Force a smaller tracheostomy tube into the stoma

prompt: During laser surgery of the airway, a fire ignites in the endotracheal tube. What is the first action?

options.text: Stop gas flow and remove the tube
Pour saline down the tube and continue the case
Increase FiO2 to 1.0 to support oxygenation
Deflate the cuff and leave the tube in place

explanation: In an airway fire, stop ventilation and gas flow, remove the burning tube, and flood the airway with saline. Then re-establish the airway and assess the injury by bronchoscopy.

prompt: A patient develops wheeze, stridor, hypotension, and hives minutes after an IV antibiotic. What is the first drug to give?

Intramuscular epinephrine
Inhaled albuterol by nebulizer
Methylprednisolone given intravenously

explanation: Intramuscular epinephrine (0.3-0.5 mg in adults, anterolateral thigh) is first-line for anaphylaxis, reversing bronchospasm, airway edema, and hypotension. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.

distractorExplanations.a: Antihistamines help hives but not airway edema or shock.
distractorExplanations.c: Albuterol treats bronchospasm only, not upper-airway edema or shock.
distractorExplanations.d: Steroids act too slowly to be first-line.

prompt: A patient found unresponsive has a respiratory rate of 4/min, pinpoint pupils, and a palpable pulse. What should the therapist do first?

options.text: Start chest compressions at 100-120 per minute
Give naloxone and wait for breathing to return
Apply a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min
Ventilate by bag-mask and give naloxone

explanation: Respiratory arrest with a pulse needs ventilation first: bag-mask with oxygen, plus naloxone to reverse the opioid. Compressions are not indicated while a pulse is present.

distractorExplanations.b: Naloxone can take minutes; the patient needs ventilation now.
distractorExplanations.c: A non-rebreather supplies oxygen but does not ventilate.

prompt: A pregnant patient with carbon monoxide poisoning has COHb 32% and had a brief loss of consciousness. What should the therapist recommend?

options.text: Nasal cannula at 4 L/min
Discharge once COHb falls below 10%
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
Observation in room air with repeat COHb levels

explanation: Hyperbaric oxygen is considered for severe CO poisoning: loss of consciousness, neurologic signs, COHb above about 25% (lower in pregnancy), or cardiac ischemia. It shortens COHb half-life and may reduce delayed neurologic effects.

distractorExplanations.a: Low-flow oxygen is inadequate for severe CO poisoning.
distractorExplanations.b: The COHb level alone does not define safety; loss of consciousness and pregnancy point to HBO.
distractorExplanations.d: Withholding oxygen is never appropriate in CO poisoning.

A bag-mask only, without monitoring, to move faster
Turning off the ventilator alarms for the trip

distractorExplanations.d: Alarms must stay on; they are the safety net in transit.

Continue the procedure while watching the monitor closely

prompt: After thoracentesis of 1.8 L, a patient develops cough, dyspnea, and new crackles on the treated side. What is the most likely cause?

options.text: Tension pneumothorax on the treated side
Pulmonary embolism from immobility
Pleural infection introduced by the needle
Re-expansion pulmonary edema

explanation: Rapid removal of a large volume (commonly over 1-1.5 L) can cause re-expansion pulmonary edema on the treated side. Give oxygen and support, and limit drainage volumes in future.

prompt: A 2-year-old suddenly coughs and wheezes after eating peanuts, and breath sounds are reduced with wheeze on the right side only. What is most likely?

options.text: An asthma exacerbation
Croup
Foreign-body aspiration into the right bronchus
Bronchiolitis from a viral lower respiratory infection

explanation: Sudden choking with one-sided wheeze or reduced breath sounds in a toddler suggests a bronchial foreign body, more often on the right. Recommend inspiratory and expiratory films and rigid bronchoscopy.

distractorExplanations.a: Asthma causes bilateral wheeze, not one-sided findings.
distractorExplanations.b: Croup gives a barking cough and stridor, not one-sided wheeze.
distractorExplanations.d: Bronchiolitis is viral, with a gradual onset and bilateral findings.

prompt: A conscious adult in a restaurant cannot speak or cough and is clutching the throat. What should be done?

options.text: Abdominal thrusts until the object clears
A blind finger sweep of the mouth
Back blows only, as for an infant
Encourage the person to keep coughing forcefully

explanation: Severe airway obstruction in a conscious adult is treated with abdominal thrusts (chest thrusts if pregnant or obese). If the person becomes unresponsive, start CPR and look in the mouth before giving breaths.

distractorExplanations.b: Blind sweeps can push the object deeper.
distractorExplanations.c: Back blows alone are the infant technique, not the adult standard.
distractorExplanations.d: Coughing helps only in mild obstruction, when the person can still cough.

prompt: A patient coughs up about 400 mL of blood within an hour, and the source is the right lung. How should the patient be positioned?

options.text: Supine with the head of the bed flat
Right side down, bleeding lung dependent
Left side down, healthy lung dependent
Prone, to help drain blood out of the airways

explanation: Placing the bleeding lung down keeps blood from spilling into the healthy lung. Secure the airway (a large tube for bronchoscopy, or selective intubation), then localize the bleed by bronchoscopy or angiography.

distractorExplanations.a: Lying flat lets blood spill into both lungs.

distractorExplanations.d: Prone positioning makes airway control and suction harder.

prompt: A ventilated patient keeps having moderate hemoptysis while awaiting bronchial artery embolization. Which inhaled medication may the physician order to reduce the bleeding?

options.text: Nebulized N-acetylcysteine
Nebulized dornase alfa
Nebulized albuterol
Nebulized tranexamic acid

explanation: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic that stabilizes clot, and nebulized TXA has been shown to reduce hemoptysis volume. It is a bridge, not a substitute for bronchoscopic or angiographic control.

distractorExplanations.c: Albuterol relaxes the airways and does not reduce bleeding.

Immediate (red)
Expectant (black)

Immediate intubation in the emergency room
Chest physiotherapy with postural drainage

Order a stat portable chest radiograph to look for a cause
Bag with 100% O2 and check for DOPE causes
